name: Safranbolu
desc: The Ottoman merchant town survives almost whole: timber-framed houses with white plaster fronts stepping down three valleys, a covered bazaar of coppersmiths and saddlers, and the 1645 Cinci hamam still taking customers. Çarşı fills with day-trippers by eleven, so walk it early, when woodsmoke hangs in the valley and the shutters are still shut.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov; snow in Jan–Feb is photogenic but shops close by dark
tip: Climb to Hıdırlık hill at sunset for the rooftop view — coaches cannot get up there, so the terrace stays local.
rev: Visitors call it the best-preserved Ottoman town in the country, then complain about weekend coach crowds, twenty shops selling identical saffron lokum, and cobbles that punish soft shoes.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 220 km north via Gerede; intercity buses from Ankara and Istanbul run to Karabük, 10 km away

name: Yörük Köyü
desc: Nine kilometres east of Safranbolu, a village of tall konaks built by a settled Yörük community that grew rich on trade and then largely left. Stone lanes, painted ceilings behind unlocked doors, and a communal stone laundry with its wood-fired cauldron. On a weekday you may meet nobody but the tea-house men and a few cats.
season: May–Oct; the lanes ice over in winter and most konaks shut
tip: Ask at the tea house for the key to the çamaşırhane, the communal laundry — it is kept locked and nobody offers it unprompted.
rev: People who come say it is Safranbolu without the crowds; the recurring gripes are that half the houses are shuttered, opening hours are whatever the caretaker decides, and there is nowhere to eat.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then Safranbolu and 9 km east on the Kastamonu road; village dolmuş is rare, a taxi from Çarşı is the practical option

name: Bulak (Mencilis) Cave
desc: A six-kilometre cave system in the hill above Bulak village, of which about four hundred metres is lit and railed. Three levels, an underground stream you hear before you see, and columns the colour of wet clay. The climb to the mouth is a few hundred steps up an open slope with the whole Safranbolu valley behind you.
season: Apr–Nov; the access steps are treacherous in ice and the cave shuts in bad weather
tip: Bring a jacket — it holds around 12 °C inside all year, and the stair up to the entrance is the warm-up, not the visit.
todo: The lit gallery to the stream
Count the steps to the mouth
Valley view from the entrance terrace
rev: Most rate it good value and quieter than the famous caves, while noting the steep approach steps, permanently wet handrails and lighting that defeats phone cameras.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then Safranbolu and 8 km north-west on the Bulak road; no bus, so drive or take a taxi from Çarşı

name: Tokatlı Canyon and İncekaya Aqueduct
tr: Tokatlı Kanyonu ve İncekaya Su Kemeri
desc: A limestone gorge a hundred metres deep on Safranbolu's doorstep, crossed by a six-arch aqueduct that İzzet Mehmet Paşa built in 1797 to bring water to the town. You can walk the open water channel on top, which has no railing. Downstream a glass terrace hangs over the drop, and the canyon path continues into the trees.
season: Apr–Nov; the canyon path is slick and often closed after heavy rain
tip: Walk the aqueduct channel itself — almost everyone stops at the crystal terrace 700 m away and never crosses the arches.
rev: Walkers love the aqueduct crossing and are less kind about the terrace: a queue, a fee, plastic overshoes, and scratched glass that ruins the photograph everyone came for.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then Safranbolu and 6 km north on the Bulak road; walkable from Çarşı in about an hour uphill

name: Hadrianopolis
desc: A Roman and early Byzantine town in the fields outside Eskipazar, dug since 2003 and known for church floors paved with mosaic animals — an elephant, a griffin, horses, a peacock — under simple shelters. Baths, a villa and cisterns lie around them in cut grass. There is no ticket office and often nobody else at all.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the mosaics are sheeted over in winter and the field turns to mud
tip: Come inside working hours on a weekday — the mosaic shelters are locked and the site guard, who has the key, goes home at five.
rev: Those who make the detour rate the mosaics far above the effort, but report locked shelters outside office hours, almost no signage, and nowhere to eat nearer than Eskipazar.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 180 km north to Eskipazar off the D100; the site is 3 km from the town centre and you need a car

name: Kaymakamlar House
desc: The best-explained konak in Safranbolu: three floors of an eighteenth-century officer's house, with a stable at ground level, a summer room open to the valley, and cupboards that turn out to be washing cabinets hidden inside the panelling. Mannequins in period dress are corny, but the carpentry and the rotating door are the point.
season: All year; least crowded Nov–Mar
tip: Ask the attendant to open the concealed gusülhane inside the wall cupboard — it is not signposted and most visitors walk straight past it.
todo: Ceiling rose in the main room
rev: Visitors find it the clearest window into how these houses were lived in, while grumbling about the mannequins, the tight stairs and coach parties that fill three rooms at once.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then Safranbolu; the house is a five-minute walk uphill from the Çarşı bazaar

name: Cinci Han
desc: A 1645 caravanserai in the middle of the bazaar, two galleried storeys of stone around a courtyard where camels once stood and tea is now served. It works as a hotel, but nobody stops you walking into the yard. The hamam of the same date and the same founder is a hundred metres away.
season: All year; the stone rooms are cold Dec–Feb
tip: If you stay, insist on an upper-gallery room — the ground-floor cells were storerooms and they are still dark and damp.
todo: Look up at the vaulted galleries
rev: Guests praise the setting and the courtyard breakfast, then flag thin mattresses, sound that carries around the gallery, and rooms priced well above the town average.
entry: Free to enter the courtyard · rooms from ≈€45
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then Safranbolu; the han sits at the centre of Çarşı, two minutes from the bazaar square

name: Kastamonu Castle and Old Town
desc: A blunt stone citadel on a crag with the whole town spread below it, and under it a working Ottoman quarter: Nasrullah square and its mosque, the Münire medrese full of craft workshops, and streets of timber konaks that are lived in rather than curated. Atatürk announced the hat reform here in 1925.
season: May–Oct; Kastamonu winters are long, grey and genuinely cold
tip: The castle path starts behind the statue on the north side — the other approach road ends at a dead-end car park with no way through.
rev: Travellers like that the old town is unrestored and unpretentious; the common complaints are a steep unshaded climb to the castle, limited English signage, and shops that shut early on Sundays.
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport has a handful of flights, otherwise Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) and 240 km north on the D765; buses run hourly from Ankara

name: Ilgaz Mountain Ski Centre
desc: The black-pine ridge between Kastamonu and Çankırı, topped by Büyük Hacet at 2587 m, with lifts at Yurduntepe and Kadınçayırı around 1800 m. Runs are short and gentle by Alpine standards and the snow is reliable from January. In summer the same road gives cool forest walks and yayla meadows an hour from the coast road.
season: Jan–Mar for snow, Jun–Sep for walking; Apr–May is mud and closed lifts
tip: Ski midweek — Ankara and Kastamonu empty onto this mountain at weekends and the lift queues double the price of the day in time.
near: Yurduntepe Kayak Merkezi, Ilgaz, Kastamonu, Türkiye
todo: Büyük Hacet summit walk in summer
rev: Skiers call it decent value and family-friendly, then complain about short pistes, weekend queues, tired rental gear and hotels that charge Alpine prices for half-board.
entry: Day lift pass ≈₺600 (€13) · the road and summer trails are free
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) or Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then the D765; the ski road climbs 25 km from the Ilgaz pass and needs winter tyres

name: Valla Canyon
desc: Twelve kilometres of limestone slot in the Küre Mountains, with walls that rise more than a kilometre above the river. The through-trip is a two-day scramble with ropes, cold water and no exits, which is why almost everyone stops at the terrace above Muratbaşı and looks down at a green thread of water instead.
season: Late Jun–Sep only for the floor; the terrace is open May–Oct, snowbound in winter
tip: Do not enter the canyon without a licensed guide and a weather check — flash floods have killed walkers here, and there is no phone signal inside.
todo: Beech forest walk on the rim
rev: Trekkers rank it among the hardest and best canyons in Türkiye; the honest reports mention rescue callouts, a rough forest road to the rim, and a viewing terrace that is the whole visit for most people.
entry: Terrace free · guided canyon traverse ≈€120 per person
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport or Ankara (ESB), then 80 km north to Pınarbaşı and a rough forest road to the rim; a high-clearance car helps

name: Horma Canyon and Ilıca Waterfall
desc: Valla's approachable neighbours, both a short drive from the village of Pınarbaşı. A boardwalk bolted to the rock runs two and a half kilometres above the Horma stream, cold and loud even in August; the Ilıca waterfall drops into a mossy bowl fifteen minutes' walk from its car park. Trout restaurants sit at both ends.
season: May–Oct; the boardwalk is closed by snow and ice roughly Dec–Mar
tip: Walk Horma from the upper entrance downhill and arrange a lift back — the return climb in the gorge is the part people regret.
rev: Walkers call it one of the easiest ways to see serious canyon country, while noting slippery planks after rain, weekend picnic crowds and a boardwalk that shows its age in places.
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport, then 80 km north to Pınarbaşı via Azdavay; minibuses run from Kastamonu but not to the canyon gates

name: Cide and Gideros Cove
desc: Cide has a long grey-sand and pebble beach with almost no hotels on it, and twelve kilometres west, Gideros is a near-circular rock cove where ancient Cytorus stood — two fish restaurants, a few boats, and cliffs closing the mouth. Behind them the Loç valley runs up into the Küre forests.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; the sea is cold and rough Oct–May
tip: Gideros has no beach — you swim off the rocks or the jetty; the sand is back east at Uğurlu, and the cove restaurants want you to book in August.
rev: People describe an undeveloped stretch of Black Sea coast worth the drive, then warn about the twisting coast road, strong undertow off Cide's open beach, and everything shutting after mid-September.
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport, then 130 km north on the Azdavay road, or the coast road west from Sinop; the last hour is slow and winding

name: Mahmut Bey Mosque
desc: A plain barn of a building in Kasaba village that opens into a forest of painted wooden columns, built in 1366 and joined with pegs rather than nails. Red, black and white vegetal patterns still cover the beams and the muqarnas capitals. It became a World Heritage site in 2023 as one of five wooden hypostyle mosques.
season: All year; the village road is fine in winter but the mosque is unheated
tip: It is kept locked — phone ahead or ask in the village shop for the caretaker, who lives two streets away and will open it for you.
todo: Painted ceiling beams above the nave
rev: Everyone who gets inside calls it extraordinary; the recurring problems are the locked door, no fixed opening hours, and a low-lit interior that photographs badly without a tripod.
entry: Free · a donation to the caretaker is normal
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport, then 17 km north-west to Kasaba village on the Daday road; there is no bus, so drive or take a taxi

name: Abana
desc: A small, tidy seaside town where the mountains stop at a pebble beach and a promenade of tea gardens. Nothing much happens: fishermen mend nets, families who emigrated to Istanbul come home in August, and the fish restaurants serve hamsi in season. It is the Black Sea coast without a single tower block.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; Aug is when the town actually fills up
tip: Eat in the harbour rather than the promenade — the boats land here and the difference in a plate of hamsi is obvious.
rev: Regulars value the quiet and the cleanliness; the complaints are limited nightlife, a pebble rather than sand beach, and prices that jump in the three weeks around 15 August.
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport, then 85 km north over the Küre pass to the coast at Bozkurt; minibuses run from Kastamonu's otogar

name: Şeyh Şaban-ı Veli Complex
desc: The tomb, mosque and dervish lodge of the sixteenth-century Halveti sheikh who made Kastamonu a Sufi centre, still the town's spiritual address. Pilgrims come by the coachload to the türbe; the old lodge beside it now holds a museum of carved wooden objects, and the courtyard has a plane tree and a fountain.
season: All year; Fridays and Ramadan are busiest
tip: Go on a weekday morning — after Friday prayers the courtyard is solid with pilgrim coaches and the wooden-artefacts museum is unusable.
todo: Wooden artefacts in the old lodge
rev: Visitors describe an atmosphere that outsiders can feel too, while noting strict dress rules, no photography inside the tomb, and coaches that arrive without warning.
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport or Ankara (ESB), then the D765; the complex is a twenty-minute uphill walk from Nasrullah square

name: Küre Mountains National Park
desc: A karst massif of beech and fir between Kastamonu and the sea, riddled with sinkholes, caves and the Valla and Horma canyons. Bears and wolves live here and you will not see them; what you get is deep forest, wooden-house villages like Azdavay and Şenpazar, and trails that are marked well in some valleys and not at all in others.
season: May–Oct; snow closes the high forest roads Dec–Mar
tip: Base yourself in Azdavay or Pınarbaşı rather than Kastamonu city — the canyon gates are an hour closer and pensions there arrange guides.
rev: Walkers rate the forest among the wildest in northern Türkiye, and consistently complain about unmarked trails, patchy maps, forest roads that need clearance, and almost no English information.
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport, then 70–100 km north on the Azdavay or Pınarbaşı roads; without a car you are dependent on infrequent minibuses

name: Kastamonu Pastırma and Siyez Bulgur
desc: Kastamonu cures its pastırma in cold mountain air with a thin coat of çemen, so it tastes of meat rather than paste — a different animal from the Kayseri version. The other local staple is siyez, einkorn wheat ground into a nutty bulgur, and Taşköprü's garlic, which has protected status and a summer festival.
season: Sep–Dec for new-season pastırma; the Taşköprü garlic festival is in July
tip: Buy pastırma sliced to order at a Nasrullah square butcher, not vacuum-packed at the bus station — and ask for sırt, the back cut.
todo: Sliced sırt pastırma at the butchers
rev: Food travellers say it beats the better-known versions and costs less; the caveats are shops that close at six, few English words anywhere, and airline rules on carrying cured meat home.
entry: Free to browse · a plate of siyez pilav ≈₺150 (€3.50)
onward: Kastamonu (KFS) airport, then 40 km north-east to Taşköprü for the garlic and grain, or stay in Kastamonu for the butchers and lokantas

name: Sinop Fortress Prison
desc: A prison built inside the ancient citadel in 1887 and used until 1997, with a reputation as the place nobody escaped from. Cell blocks, exercise yards and workshops stand as they were left, walls scratched with names and dates. Sabahattin Ali did time here, and the writing about it is half of Türkiye's prison literature.
season: All year; May–Sep is pleasant, the yards are baking at midday in Jul–Aug
tip: Walk the citadel ramparts afterwards from the northern gate — the same ticket area gives you the sea view the prisoners never had.
rev: Most find the empty cells genuinely affecting; the repeated complaints are thin English captions, a few rooms roped off without explanation, and hard glare in the yards in high summer.
onward: Sinop (NOP) airport 6 km away, or Samsun Çarşamba (SZF) and 170 km west on the coast road; the prison is in the old town, walkable from the harbour

name: Hamsilos Bay
desc: A narrow green inlet cut two hundred metres into the coast, pines leaning over water so still that boats sit on their own reflections. Guides call it Türkiye's only fjord, which it is not, but the shape is odd enough to be worth the eleven kilometres from Sinop. Akliman beach and the Sarıkum lagoon are next door.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; Apr–May and Oct for walking the pine paths
tip: Swim off the rocks on the eastern arm — the head of the inlet is silty and the western picnic area is claimed by families before noon.
rev: Visitors like the shape and the shade, then note the fjord label is oversold, the picnic crowds leave litter, and the water can be murky after a storm.
entry: Free · small car park fee in summer
onward: Sinop (NOP) airport, then 11 km north-west past Akliman; city minibuses run to Akliman in summer, otherwise take a taxi

name: Erfelek Tatlıca Waterfalls
desc: Twenty-eight cascades strung along a single kilometre of stream in a beech gorge, linked by wooden stairs and bridges that cross the water again and again. None of the falls is tall, but the sequence is relentless and the air stays cold in August. The walk up and back takes about ninety minutes.
season: May–Oct; boards are icy and often closed Dec–Mar, and the flow is thin in late Aug
tip: Arrive before ten or after four — the car park fills by eleven at weekends and the narrow boardwalk becomes a single-file queue.
todo: Cold trout at the gate restaurant
rev: Almost everyone calls the walk lovely and short; the standard complaints are slippery planks after rain, weekend queues on the bridges and identical souvenir stalls at the entrance.
onward: Sinop (NOP) airport, then 35 km south-west via Erfelek town and 12 km of narrow valley road; minibuses reach Erfelek but not the falls

name: İnceburun
desc: The northernmost point of Türkiye: a low limestone cape with a small white lighthouse, a wind that never stops, and nothing else. The rock is scoured into ledges and pools, the sea is usually white where it hits them, and on a clear day the horizon is genuinely empty. It takes ten minutes and stays with you.
season: May–Oct; winter storms make the exposed cape unpleasant and the track muddy
tip: The last two kilometres are unsurfaced and rutted — leave a low car at the top and walk down, especially after rain.
todo: Rock pools on the west ledge
rev: People enjoy the emptiness and the bragging rights, while warning about the rough access track, zero facilities, and a lighthouse compound you cannot enter.
onward: Sinop (NOP) airport, then 22 km north-west past Akliman and a final gravel track; no public transport, so drive or hire a taxi to wait

name: Gerze
desc: A fishing town of wooden houses forty kilometres down the coast from Sinop, with a small harbour of blue boats, boatyards still cutting timber, and tea gardens looking straight at the sea. It made national news once for stopping a coal plant, then went back to being quiet. The pace is the attraction.
season: Jun–Sep; out of season half the seafront closes and the wind comes straight in
tip: Eat at the harbour before eight — kitchens shut early outside July and August, and the last dolmuş back to Sinop leaves around seven.
todo: Wooden houses on the back streets
rev: Visitors describe a genuinely unpolished coastal town, and mention the narrow pebble beach, limited accommodation and the highway that runs right behind the seafront.
onward: Sinop (NOP) airport, then 40 km south-east on the coast road; frequent minibuses run from Sinop otogar and stop on the main street

name: Ayancık and the Çangal Forest
desc: A timber town on the coast west of Sinop, with the Çangal fir and beech forest rising behind it — one of the wettest, greenest corners of the country. Logging roads climb to yayla meadows and the small lake at Akgöl, mist sits in the valleys most mornings, and Ayancık still weaves the linen it is named for.
season: Jun–Sep; it rains here all year and forest tracks are impassable after storms
tip: Fill the tank in Ayancık before going up — there is no fuel and no reliable phone signal once the forest road starts climbing.
rev: Those who venture up praise empty forest and cool air, and warn about rough unsigned tracks, sudden fog, and a town with few beds and fewer restaurants.
onward: Sinop (NOP) airport, then 80 km west on the coast road; minibuses reach Ayancık, but the forest needs a car with decent clearance

name: Balatlar Church
desc: A seventh-century Byzantine church wedged into the shell of a second-century Roman bath, roofless and open to the sky in a residential street above Sinop harbour. Patches of fresco survive high on the brick walls — saints' faces, ochre and blue. It has been under excavation since 2010, so what you see changes year to year.
season: Apr–Oct; the site is exposed and turns to mud in winter
tip: Go in the morning, when the light reaches the frescoes on the north wall; by afternoon that side is in deep shadow.
todo: Fresco fragments on the upper walls
Look for the current dig trench
rev: Visitors find the layering of Roman and Byzantine work fascinating and complain that half the site is fenced for excavation, explanation is minimal, and it is easy to walk past the gate.
onward: Sinop (NOP) airport, then the old town; the church is a ten-minute uphill walk from the harbour, signposted from the main street

name: Amisos Hill and Cable Car
desc: A cable car lifts you from the shore park to a pine hill above Samsun where Hellenistic chamber tombs were opened in 1995 and gave up a hoard of gold jewellery, now in the city museum. The tombs are open and empty; the reason people come is the terrace, the tea gardens and the whole bay laid out below.
season: All year; May–Oct for clear evenings, winter can be low cloud all week
tip: Ride up an hour before sunset and walk down through the tomb terrace — the last cabins down are packed with wedding parties.
todo: Cable car up at golden hour
rev: Locals and visitors agree the view is the point; complaints are queues for the cable car at weekends, overpriced tea on the terrace, and tombs with almost no interpretation.
onward: Samsun Çarşamba (SZF) airport, then 25 km west into the city; the cable-car base station is in Batıpark on the seafront tram line

name: Bandırma Vapuru Museum Ship
desc: A full-size replica of the elderly steamer that carried Atatürk from Istanbul to Samsun on 19 May 1919, the day the independence war is dated from. It sits in a park by the sea with wax figures in the saloon and a panorama museum of the campaign beside it. For Turks it is a pilgrimage; for others, a short and blunt history lesson.
season: All year; 19 May is a national holiday and the park is packed
tip: Do the panorama museum next door first — it makes sense of the ship, which takes fifteen minutes on its own.
todo: The saloon and the wax delegation
rev: Turkish visitors find it moving, foreign visitors find it small and staged, and both mention wax figures that have seen better days and sparse English labelling.
onward: Samsun Çarşamba (SZF) airport, then 25 km west; the ship is in the seafront park, one stop on the tram from the city centre

name: Kızılırmak Delta Bird Paradise
desc: Where Anatolia's longest river reaches the sea near Bafra, a mosaic of lagoons, reedbeds and wet pasture that logs well over three hundred bird species. Cernek lake has hides and a ringing station; water buffalo stand chest-deep in the channels; flamingos and pelicans pass through in numbers. It is flat, wet and very big.
season: Apr–May and Sep–Oct for migration; Jul mosquitoes are genuinely punishing
tip: Take binoculars and your own transport to the Cernek hides — the ringing station is 12 km of unpaved dyke road past the last village.
todo: Water buffalo on the dyke road
rev: Birders rate it among the best wetlands in Türkiye and warn about mosquitoes, unpaved tracks that flood, poor signage, and boatmen who quote by the boat rather than the seat.
onward: Samsun Çarşamba (SZF) airport, then 80 km west past Bafra; the delta tracks start north of the town and need your own vehicle

name: Havza Thermal Springs
desc: Hot springs that have been in use since Roman times, rising at around fifty-five degrees in an ordinary inland town on the Samsun–Amasya road. Atatürk stayed here for two weeks in May 1919 and took the cure; his hotel is now a small museum. The bathing itself is unglamorous municipal hamams and hotel pools, and it works.
season: Oct–Apr is the point of a thermal town; Jul–Aug is too hot to enjoy it
tip: Ask for a private küvet room at a hotel spa rather than the public pool if you want quiet — they cost little more and include a soaking tub.
todo: Atatürk's rooms at the old hotel
Steam rising off the town in winter
rev: Turkish spa-goers rate the water highly, while noting tired facilities, separate men's and women's hours that catch couples out, and a town with little else to do.
entry: Public bath ≈₺150 (€3.50) · hotel spa packages more
onward: Samsun Çarşamba (SZF) airport, then 110 km south-west on the Amasya road; buses between Samsun and Amasya stop in Havza

name: Ladik Lake
desc: A shallow reed-ringed lake under the Akdağ ridge, known for floating islands of matted reed that drift across the water when the wind turns. Storks work the shallows, fishermen push flat boats through the channels, and a boardwalk and a few cafés sit on the south shore. It is an hour's detour off the Samsun–Amasya road.
season: Apr–Jun for birds and green, Sep–Oct for calm; Jan–Feb it can freeze at the edges
tip: Go early — the reed islands move with the morning breeze and by afternoon the light on the water is flat and hazy.
rev: Visitors find it peaceful and photogenic, then mention litter at the picnic areas, a lakeside road with no proper viewpoints, and very little to do beyond an hour's stop.
onward: Samsun Çarşamba (SZF) airport, then 90 km south-west via Havza to Ladik; buses on the Samsun–Amasya route pass the turn-off

name: Şahinkaya Canyon
desc: The Kızılırmak backed up behind the Altınkaya dam has flooded a gorge into a corridor of green water between three-hundred-metre cliffs. Small boats run from the village jetty for an hour up the canyon and back, and a glass terrace juts out over the drop above. Eagles use the thermals against the rock face.
season: May–Oct; boats stop running in winter and the access road ices over
tip: Boats only leave when they fill, so arrive at midday or expect to pay for the whole boat yourself.
todo: Boat trip up the flooded gorge
rev: Day-trippers call the boat hour genuinely dramatic; the recurring problems are waiting for a boat to fill, a scratched glass terrace, and a long slow drive from Samsun.
onward: Samsun Çarşamba (SZF) airport, then 130 km west via Vezirköprü and 30 km of hill road to the jetty; a car is essential

name: Amasya Rock Tombs and Yalıboyu Houses
tr: Amasya Kral Kaya Mezarları ve Yalıboyu Evleri
desc: Five vast tombs of the Pontic kings are cut straight into the cliff above the town, hollow rooms with a walkway carved around them. Below, Ottoman timber houses stand with their feet in the Yeşilırmak and their reflections in it. At night the cliff and the tombs are floodlit and the whole valley looks staged.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; Jul–Aug is hot in the closed valley, Jan–Feb cold and grey
tip: Photograph the houses from the north bank in the late afternoon, then climb to the tombs after dark when the floodlights are on and the stairs are empty.
todo: Climb the stair to the royal tombs
rev: Nearly everyone rates Amasya's setting above its museums, and mentions the steep tomb stairway, a loud road on the south bank, and cafés on the waterfront charging tourist prices.
onward: Amasya Merzifon (MZH) airport 45 km away, or Samsun (SZF) 130 km; the train from Samsun stops in Amasya and the old town is a short walk from the station

name: Harşena Castle
desc: The fortress on the crag three hundred metres above Amasya, rebuilt so many times that Pontic, Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman masonry sit in the same wall. The real find is Cilanbolu: a rock-cut stairway plunging down a shaft to a cistern, unlit at the bottom. The view over the tombs, the river and the whole valley is the best in town.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the summit road is icy in winter and the walk up is brutal in Jul–Aug heat
tip: Take a torch for the Cilanbolu water shaft — around 150 steps down into black rock with no lighting and no handrail at the bottom.
todo: Cilanbolu water shaft with a torch
rev: Visitors rate the panorama and the tunnel highly, while flagging a narrow road with nowhere to pass, a scramble on loose stone at the top, and restoration work that closes sections without notice.
onward: Amasya Merzifon (MZH) airport, then Amasya; the castle road climbs 5 km from the western edge of town, or walk up in an hour from Yalıboyu

name: Ferhat and Şirin Water Channel
desc: An irrigation channel cut into the rock face above the Yeşilırmak, ancient engineering that legend hands to Ferhat the stonemason, who was told to carve water through a mountain before he could marry Şirin. You walk the ledge beside the channel with the valley dropping away and Amasya laid out downstream. It takes half an hour and few people bother.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the ledge is slippery after rain and exposed in summer heat
tip: Start from the western end near the picnic area — the eastern approach involves a scramble that families regret halfway along.
todo: Look down on the Yeşilırmak bend
Read the Ferhat and Şirin legend first
rev: Walkers enjoy the quiet and the drop, and mention crumbling handrails, no shade at all, and an unmarked start that costs most people twenty minutes of searching.
onward: Amasya Merzifon (MZH) airport, then Amasya; the channel starts about 3 km west of the centre on the north bank, reachable by taxi or a riverside walk

name: Borabay Lake
desc: A landslide-dammed lake at eight hundred metres, ringed by beech forest so close that the water is green with it. A path loops the shore in under an hour, wooden bungalows and a trout restaurant sit at one end, and mist lies on the surface most mornings. It is the coolest place in the province in August.
season: May–Oct; the forest road is often snowbound Dec–Mar
tip: Stay the night in a bungalow if you can — the lake at dawn, before the day-trippers from Taşova arrive, is a different place entirely.
rev: Visitors describe genuine forest calm on weekdays and a picnic circus at summer weekends, with complaints about a narrow twisting access road and basic bungalows.
entry: Small vehicle fee at the gate
onward: Amasya Merzifon (MZH) airport, then 90 km east via Taşova and 15 km of forest road; there is no bus to the lake

name: Amasya Apple Orchards
desc: The misket apple that put Amasya on the province's coat of arms is small, striped red over yellow, tart and strongly scented — nothing like a supermarket apple. Orchards line the Yeşilırmak valley and the Suluova plain, and from late September roadside tables sell them by the crate along with dried okra strung like beads.
season: Late Sep–Nov for harvest; blossom in late Apr is the other reason to come
tip: Buy from a roadside grower rather than a town shop and ask for misket by name — most stalls also sell modern varieties that look better and taste of nothing.
todo: Buy misket apples at a roadside stall
Blossom in the valley in late April
rev: Food travellers say the apple deserves the reputation, while warning that many stalls sell ordinary varieties under the local name and that the season is short.
entry: Free · a kilo at a roadside stall ≈₺40 (€1)
onward: Amasya Merzifon (MZH) airport, then the Suluova and Amasya road; the stalls line the D100 and the valley road, so you need a car to stop

name: Hattusa
desc: The Hittite capital spread over six kilometres of high grassland: a Lion Gate, a Sphinx Gate above the Yerkapı tunnel that runs right through the rampart, and the Great Temple's foundations with a green stone nobody can explain. A one-way loop road links them. The scale and the emptiness are what stay with you.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the plateau is 1000 m, freezing in winter and shadeless in Jul–Aug
tip: Drive the loop anticlockwise and take Yerkapı first — by midday the tunnel is a queue and the ridge wind is hard work.
todo: Great Temple and the green stone
rev: Visitors are impressed by the scale and frustrated by how little stands above knee height; the standard gripes are no shade, a 6 km circuit that punishes anyone without a car, and thin signage.
entry: ₺600 (≈€13) joint with Yazılıkaya · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 200 km east via Sungurlu, or Amasya Merzifon (MZH) 130 km; buses reach Sungurlu, then a taxi covers the last 30 km

name: Yazılıkaya
desc: Two natural rock chambers two kilometres from Hattusa, their walls carved with a procession of more than sixty Hittite gods meeting in the middle — the open-air sanctuary of the empire. In the narrow second chamber the god Sharruma has his arm around King Tudhaliya, and a sword god is driven into the rock like a blade.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; afternoon light suits the reliefs, winter can be snowbound
tip: Come in the afternoon — morning light leaves the main chamber's reliefs flat, and the low sun brings the processions out of the rock.
todo: Procession of gods in Chamber A
rev: Most call it the highlight of the Hittite trip and better preserved than Hattusa, while noting the site takes barely half an hour, offers no shade, and the reliefs are weathering visibly.
entry: Included in the Hattusa ticket · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then Boğazkale; Yazılıkaya is 2 km north-east of the village and signposted from the Hattusa loop

name: Alacahöyük
desc: A mound occupied since the Bronze Age, entered through a Sphinx Gate with a double-headed eagle cut into the jamb. Behind it lie thirteen royal Hatti tombs that produced the sun discs and bull standards now used as symbols of Anatolia — the originals are in Ankara, but the shaft graves are open and a small museum holds the rest.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the site is open ground with no shade in summer
tip: See the site museum first — the reconstruction drawings make sense of the tomb shafts, which otherwise look like empty pits.
todo: Sphinx Gate and the eagle relief
Sun disc replicas in the museum
rev: Archaeology-minded visitors find it essential context for Hattusa; others note the famous finds are all in Ankara, the site is small, and the village has almost no facilities.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 210 km east via Sungurlu, or 45 km north of Boğazkale by road; no public transport to the village

name: Şapinuva
desc: The Hittites' second royal centre, in the fields outside Ortaköy, where a burnt building baked and preserved more than three thousand cuneiform tablets. Massive cut-stone foundations run across a slope of stubble, trenches are open, and the dig is still going. There is no visitor centre and often nobody but the site guard.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the excavation season is summer, when you may see work in progress
tip: Visit on a weekday in July or August and you can watch the dig itself — the team will usually explain what they are lifting.
rev: Hittite enthusiasts find it thrilling to stand in a working excavation; everyone else reports little standing above knee height, no shade, no signage and no facilities.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) or Amasya Merzifon (MZH) airport, then Çorum and 55 km south-east to Ortaköy; the site is 2 km from the town and needs a car

name: İncesu Canyon
desc: A twelve-kilometre limestone gorge south of Ortaköy with poplars along the stream, a road hugging one bank and a walking track on the other. Byzantine monks cut a church and cells into the cliff, reachable on a rough path. It is the green surprise of a dry province and almost nobody outside Çorum knows it.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the stream shrinks by late August and the track floods after storms
tip: The rock-cut church is about 1.5 km past the last picnic table on the left bank — nothing marks it from the road, so watch the cliff line.
rev: Visitors call it a genuine find and complain about litter at the picnic areas, an unmarked and eroded path to the church, and a narrow road with nowhere to turn a car.
onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then Çorum and 55 km south-east to Ortaköy; the canyon road runs south from the town and needs your own car

name: Çorum Leblebi
desc: Roasted chickpeas are a national snack, and Çorum is where they are taken seriously: a whole arcade of leblebi shops, sacks of white, yellow and double-roasted, plus salted, chilli and sugar-coated versions nobody outside the town admits to buying. The process runs over several days in wood-fired drums and the smell fills the street.
season: All year; the shops are busiest around the Hittite festival in July
tip: Ask for çifte kavrulmuş — double-roasted — and taste before you buy; every shop will hand you a scoop, and the difference between them is real.
todo: Taste your way down Leblebiciler arcade
rev: Visitors enjoy the free tasting and the theatre of the roasting drums, then note the shops all look identical, prices vary wildly, and the town itself is short on other sights.
onward: Amasya Merzifon (MZH) airport 90 km, or Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) 240 km; the leblebi arcade is in the centre, a few minutes from the otogar shuttle stop

name: Ballıca Cave
desc: A cave on a hilltop near Pazar with almost seven hundred metres of walkway across two levels and eight halls, best known for stalagmites shaped like giant mushrooms — flat caps grown by dripping from a high roof. Bats live in the upper galleries and the air is famously easy on the lungs.
season: All year; the cave holds a steady temperature, but the hill road is awkward in ice
tip: Go early on a weekday — coach parties fill the narrow walkway and there is no way to pass anyone once you are inside.
todo: View over the valley from the entrance
rev: Reviewers rank it among the country's best caves, with the usual caveats: around three hundred steps, coloured lighting that ruins photographs, and coaches blocking the hilltop car park at weekends.
onward: Tokat (TJK) airport, then 30 km south-west via Pazar and 7 km up a hill road; buses reach Pazar but not the cave

name: Tokat Castle and Latifoğlu Konak
desc: The castle sits on a rock spur over the town with twenty-eight towers, rock-cut cisterns and a restored path to a viewing platform on the edge. Ten minutes below, the Latifoğlu Konak is an eighteenth-century mansion whose painted ceilings and Baroque-influenced pasha's room are the finest interiors in the region.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the castle climb is unpleasant in Jul–Aug heat
tip: Do the konak in the middle of the day and the castle late — the platform faces west and the town below turns gold about an hour before sunset.
todo: Viewing platform on the castle spur
Painted pasha's room in the konak
rev: Visitors praise the konak's interiors and the castle view, while noting steep uneven steps, sections of the fortress fenced for restoration, and irregular opening hours at the mansion.
onward: Tokat (TJK) airport 20 km away, or Samsun (SZF) 240 km; both sites are in the centre and walkable from the main square

name: Niksar
desc: Ancient Neocaesarea, later the Danişmend capital, on a shelf above the Kelkit valley with walnut and cherry orchards below the walls. The citadel is half ruin and half neighbourhood, the Yağıbasan medrese claims to be Anatolia's first, and the town's mosques carry carved doors nobody queues to see.
season: Apr–Jun for blossom and cherries, Sep–Oct for walnuts; hot and dusty in Jul–Aug
tip: Buy cherries in June from the orchard stalls on the Erbaa road — Niksar's are what Istanbul greengrocers charge a premium for.
todo: Cherries and walnuts from the roadside
rev: Travellers like the unforced, lived-in feel and note that monuments are locked as often as open, restoration is patchy, and there is little accommodation beyond basic town hotels.
onward: Tokat (TJK) airport, then 55 km north-east on the Erbaa road; regular minibuses run from Tokat otogar

name: Zile
desc: A castle on an artificial mound where Caesar beat Pharnaces in 47 BC and reported it in three words — veni, vidi, vici. The arc of a Roman theatre is built into the mound's flank, houses have grown over the rest, and a clock tower stands on top. Below it a working bazaar sells pekmez and the town's own leblebi.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the mound is exposed and hot in Jul–Aug
tip: Walk up through the old quarter instead of driving — the theatre arcs are embedded in the house walls along the way and you miss them from the road.
todo: Roman theatre arcs in the lanes
rev: Visitors enjoy the layers of history in an ordinary market town, and mention that nothing is explained on site, the castle is fenced in places, and the famous inscription is a modern plaque.
onward: Tokat (TJK) airport, then 65 km west on the Turhal road; minibuses run from Tokat and Amasya

name: Sebastopolis
desc: A Roman city sitting inside the village of Sulusaray, so the excavation trenches run between houses and gardens. Bath walls, column drums and mosaic floors under cover, with hot spring water that the Romans used and the villagers still do. Digging restarted recently, and the site changes shape from one season to the next.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the fields turn to mud in winter and there is no shade in summer
tip: Ask at the muhtar's office if the covered mosaic shelter is locked — someone in the village always has the key.
rev: Amateur archaeologists like ruins woven into a living village; the common complaints are a site fenced in pieces, half-excavated trenches, and gates that are locked with nobody obvious to ask.
onward: Tokat (TJK) airport, then 68 km south-west via Artova; there is one minibus a day from Tokat, so a car is much easier

name: Almus Lake
desc: The Yeşilırmak dammed in 1966 into a long lake between forested hills east of Tokat, with trout farms on the inlets, lakeside restaurants built over the water on stilts, and boats for hire in summer. The road along the north shore is the reason to come — pine, water and almost no traffic.
season: May–Oct; the water level drops noticeably by late summer
tip: Order the trout at a stilt restaurant on the far shore rather than the ones by the dam wall — same fish, half the coach traffic.
todo: Hire a boat for an hour
rev: Locals rate the fish and the quiet; visitors note that the shoreline is a reservoir rather than a natural lake, litter builds up at picnic spots, and swimming is discouraged.
onward: Tokat (TJK) airport, then 35 km east on the Almus road; minibuses run from Tokat to Almus town but not around the lake

name: Tokat Kebabı
desc: Lamb ribs, aubergine, tomato, potato, whole garlic cloves and a pointed pepper threaded onto a flat skewer with a piece of tail fat, stood upright in a wood-fired oven for an hour. The bread underneath catches everything that drips. It is ordered by weight, shared, and better in Tokat than anywhere else.
season: All year; ovens are lit from late morning and the best kitchens sell out by two
tip: Order by weight for two people and phone an hour ahead — good ovens will not start a skewer for a single portion.
todo: Kebap by weight at a wood-fired oven
Tokat yaprak sarma as a starter
rev: Visitors call it worth the detour and warn that portions are large, the good places close in the afternoon, and vegetarians have almost nothing to order.
entry: ≈₺450 (€10) per person in a kebap salonu
onward: Tokat (TJK) airport 20 km away, or Samsun (SZF) 240 km; the kebap houses cluster around the old bazaar in the town centre
